bodyText: Preclinical cancer research requires reproducible protocols and validated cell lines. Multiple studies published in Nature and PLOS Medicine demonstrate that statistical power and sample size determination are critical to avoid false discovery rates in oncology drug development.

bodyText: 'It doesn't work like that': India coach keeps suspense over Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's chances in playing XI | Cricket News - The Times of India Edition IN IN US UK GCC English English हिन्दी मराठी ಕನ್ನಡ தமிழ் বাংলা മലയാളം తెలుగు ગુજરાતી Weather Sign In TOI Today's ePaper Live News Sports News Cricket News 'It doesn't work like that': India coach keeps suspense over Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's chances in playing XI Trending Dilip Mahadu Gavit Sandeep Haney Shikhar Mohan Anjanaben Bumbadiya Indian Bowlers Record Nayanika Sanga Jharkhand Lawn Bowl Players Equestrian Federation Of India Steve Smith SA20 Auction Dilip Mahadu Gavit Sandeep Haney Shikhar Mohan Anjanaben Bumbadiya Indian Bowlers Record Nayanika Sanga Jharkhand Lawn Bowl Players Equestrian Federation Of India Steve Smith SA20 Auction Dilip Mahadu Gavit Sandeep Haney Shikhar Mohan Anjanaben Bumbadiya Indian Bowlers Record Nayanika Sanga Jharkhand Lawn Bowl Players Equestrian Federation Of India Steve Smith SA20 Auction 'It doesn't work like that': India coach keeps suspense over Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's chances in playing XI Edited by Hijam Raju Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Oct 23, 2026, 12:58 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small Medium Large Print Vaibhav Sooryavanshi NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak has kept the suspense alive over Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's chances of playing in the second T20I against New Zealand, insisting that the team management's selection decisions must be viewed in the larger interest of the side. With Ishan Kishan ruled out of Saturday's match due to injury, the 15-year-old batting sensation could be in contention, but Kotak backed current openers Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma. Kishan has been ruled out of the second T20I after sustaining a low-grade right adductor strain during India's four-wicket victory in the series opener. The BCCI medical team is monitoring his progress. Watch Shreyas Iyer press conference: On Sanju Samson v Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Bhuvneshwar Kumar and more Sooryavanshi, who has been on the sidelines since the Asian Games , is among the possible options as India prepare to face New Zealand at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. However, Kotak stressed that selection cannot be driven by social media demands. "...there is a lot of speculation in social media about the three openers. So, sometimes, social media should also appreciate that the team management calls are for the good of the team. Because, people want to play their own 11. It doesn't work like that," Kotak said on the eve of the second T20I. 'Sanju is outstanding': Kotak backs openers Kotak reserved special praise for Samson, who smashed 67 off 33 balls in the opening match, while Abhishek Sharma contributed 29 off just 12 deliveries. Their 93-run opening stand laid the foundation for India's successful chase of 226. "Sanju is outstanding, he is a power-packed player. The way he approached the game yesterday. There are so many runs (to chase). If you ever put yourself in the place of a batsman and think that you have to hit three or four sixes in the first two overs, you will also be afraid of getting out. "If you get out early in two or three games, you would think you would get dropped. So, overcoming all that and the intent (openers) they are showing, that excites me. "Really, it is amazing that on top of power, talent and intent and everything, they are controlling their minds also. To get them into that fearless attitude, it is unbelievable," Kotak said. Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines Kishan's absence opens selection question New Zealand posted 225/4 in the first T20I, with Glenn Phillips scoring an unbeaten 82 off 40 balls. India recovered from a brief middle-order wobble to complete the chase in 19.4 overs, with Shreyas Iyer making 42 and Naman Dhir remaining unbeaten on 42 off 15 balls. Kishan's absence leaves India with a selection decision ahead of the second match. Sooryavanshi's inclusion remains a possibility, but Kotak's comments underline the team's faith in Samson and Abhishek, whose fearless approach proved decisive in the series opener. bodyText:
Which school board is right for your child? Is private coaching necessary for competitive entrance exams? What is the process for admission to a college abroad? What course should my child pursue as AI threatens to transform jobs? Send your questions and our panel of education experts will respond with clear guidance

In a striking development in Lucknow, hoardings targeting Samajwadi Party leader Akhilesh Yadav have emerged, linking him to controversial gangster-politicians. This controversial move followed Yadav's visit to convicted politician Mohammad Azam Khan, raising eyebrows and criticism from the BJP. Yadav claims the ruling party is fabricating charges against Khan and his kin, citing a harsh political onslaught by the BJP as the motive.

India’s Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade secure at least a bronze medal in mixed doubles at the Asian Table Tennis Championships, defeating South Korea 3-2 in the quarterfinals. India win a mixed doubles medal at the event for the first time since 1954. The duo will face Japan’s Sora Matsushima and Miwa Harimoto in the semifinals for a place in the final.

A word familiar in parts of Maharashtra is travelling to audiences who may never have encountered the ritual. Back home, meanwhile, Gondhal has been getting on with the less glamorous business of surviving.

Amazon has decided not to proceed with its plans for developing four data centres in Virginia. The company will instead donate roughly 25 acres of the site to Loudoun County for community facilities. This agreement includes a contribution of $5 million towards the county's affordable housing initiatives. The decision comes after feedback from local leaders and the community regarding the proposed data centres.

Asian Para Games 2026 Day 5 Live: India continued its impressive run at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya, adding 26 medals on Day 4 to take its overall tally to 88, including 21 gold, 26 silver and 41 bronze medals. The Indian contingent remained fourth in the standings, moving closer to the 100-medal milestone.Head Coach Satyanarayan praised the athletes’ determination and performances, highlighting the team’s growing strength in para-sports. He expressed confidence that India could cross the 100-medal mark before the Games conclude.Sheetal Devi emerged as one of the standout performers, winning gold in the women’s individual compound archery event and the mixed team event alongside Toman Kumar. Swati Chaudhary also created history by securing India’s first-ever medal in the Women’s W1 Individual archery event, taking silver after losing 4–6 to China’s Mengkan Cen.India recorded another podium sweep in the Men’s High Jump T42/T63, with Shailesh Kumar winning gold with a Games-record 1.89m jump, Varun Singh Bhati taking silver and Rahul claiming bronze.Para-athletics also saw gold medals for Suvarna Raj, Anjanaben Bumbadiya and Dilip Mahadu Gavit, while Jayanti Behera won silver. Para-swimming added three medals, with Kapil Kumar taking silver and Swatik Patil and Tejas Nandkumar winning bronze.

bodyText: Dark homes, dry taps, idle factories: Gurgaon hit by 16-hour power cuts amid strike | Gurgaon News - The Times of India Edition IN IN US UK GCC English English हिन्दी मराठी ಕನ್ನಡ தமிழ் বাংলা മലയാളം తెలుగు ગુજરાતી Weather Sign In TOI Today's ePaper Live News City News gurgaon News Dark homes, dry taps, idle factories: Gurgaon hit by 16-hour power cuts amid strike Trending Bengaluru Arrest Delhi AQI Raihan Vadra Saurav Das Uddhav Thackeray Unnao Murder Case Bengaluru Arrest Delhi AQI Raihan Vadra Saurav Das Uddhav Thackeray Unnao Murder Case Bengaluru Arrest Delhi AQI Raihan Vadra Saurav Das Uddhav Thackeray Unnao Murder Case Dark homes, dry taps, idle factories: Gurgaon hit by 16-hour power cuts amid strike TNN / Updated: Oct 23, 2026, 14:26 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small Medium Large Print Thousands of households in Gurgaon faced power and water outages due to a strike by electricity department employees. GURGAON: Thousands of households went without electricity and water, nearly 1,800 manufacturing units faced disruption, and residents took to the streets as a three-day strike by Haryana's electricity department employees crippled power supply across Gurgaon on Thursday. With breakdown complaints going unattended, inverters running out of charge and industrial units struggling to keep production lines operational, the disruption exposed the city's dependence on an uninterrupted electricity supply for even its most basic needs. The strike, called to protest the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission's (HERC) decision to grant a parallel electricity distribution licence to private company Eleven Power for Gurgaon and Nuh, began affecting supplies from Wednesday night. DHBVN employees during the strike on Thursday By Thursday, power cuts had spread across residential colonies, industrial clusters and rural areas, with residents complaining that repeated calls to electricity officials and helplines had failed to bring relief. In several localities, prolonged outages also hit water supply as electricity-dependent boosting stations and household motors stopped functioning. While some residents managed with water stored in tanks, others said their reserves would last only a few hours. In industrial areas, manufacturers turned to diesel generator sets, but these offered only temporary relief, with prolonged use restricted by overheating, cooling requirements and air pollution control norms. The scale of the disruption was reflected in the complaints received by Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam (DHBVN). An official said the department received more than 3,000 complaints within the first 12 hours of the strike, while DHBVN's helplines received around 5,000 outage complaints on Thursday. Residents, however, alleged that neither the helplines nor the officials responsible for local supply were responding adequately. Gurgaon, which has around 8.5 lakh electricity consumers, saw widespread disruption, particularly in Old Gurgaon. Residents said more than 50,000 households in the area were affected on Thursday, with several localities continuing to face outages even after hours of waiting. The agitation also affected Faridabad and Nuh, where residential areas and industrial units reported power cuts. Industrialists said repeated calls to DHBVN officials had failed to resolve the disruption, leaving workers and machinery idle No electricity, no water For thousands of families, the immediate concern was no longer just the absence of electricity but the inability to carry out everyday activities, from cooking and studying to securing drinking water. In Sector 9A, around 6,000 families were affected after power supply snapped around 3.30am on Thursday. The outage also affected the boosting station supplying the area, leaving households without water. More than 16 hours later, supply had still not been restored, according to Suraj Bhola, general secretary of the Sector 9A residents' welfare association (RWA). “I have called the officials nearly 50 times, but nobody is responding. There is no electricity at our homes. Inverters have run out, and now there is no water either because the boosting station is affected. How are people supposed to manage their daily needs?” Bhola said. - General picture of Industrial workers.______________Picture by TOI He alleged that the junior engineer was not answering calls, while the sub-divisional officer had cited the strike. The helpline number provided by the district administration had also failed to secure relief, he said. With no clarity on when electricity would return, residents were unable to plan their day or arrange alternative water supplies. Tankers, he added, were also difficult to find. In Hari Nagar, more than 7,000 families were affected after power supply went off around 10pm on Wednesday and remained disrupted for more than 16 hours, residents said. The accompanying water shortage left families struggling to meet basic needs. “People are suffering in their homes, children are struggling to study, and nobody is listening to us. Junior engineer (JE) and SDO are not answering calls. The office has been locked, and there is nobody available to address the complaints,” said Sumit Gujjar, Hari Nagar RWA president. While acknowledging employees' right to protest, Gujjar questioned the impact of the agitation on ordinary residents. “If employees have an issue with the govt, they should take it up with the govt instead of leaving residents without electricity and water,” he said. The uncertainty over restoration was equally distressing for residents of housing societies, where backup systems could not meet every household's needs. At Zara Aavaas, an affordable housing society, residents said power had been unavailable since 5.30am. The backup system covered essential services such as lifts but did not provide electricity to individual flats. Hemant Sharma, a resident, said the outage had created additional difficulties as pollution levels rose and restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) came into force. “On one hand, pollution levels are increasing and GRAP restrictions are in place, while on the other, the prolonged power outage has forced people to run diesel gensets. Many residents have to work from home, but how are they supposed to work without electricity for so many hours? It is even more difficult for people with medical conditions who may depend on electrical equipment or need a comfortable indoor environment,” he said. Residents of Lotus Homz also struggled as the outage continued through the day. “There has been no power supply since 5am. It has become difficult to manage even basic household chores. Even inverter ran out of battery and I had to cook dinner using the light from my mobile phone. We don’t even know when the electricity will be restored. The management has asked residents to move to the community hall, but while we somehow managed today, we don’t know what will happen tomorrow if the power supply remains disrupted,” said resident Anu Gulati. In Rajendra Park, Bhimgarh Kheri and areas near Gurgaon railway station, residents who had been without electricity since 10am staged a protest near the railway station road bridge on Thursday evening. By around 8pm, with the outage stretching to nearly 10 hours, a large number of men and women had taken to the road and raised slogans against the power department. Police personnel reached the spot to pacify the protesters, but residents refused to disperse until electricity was restored. They said the outage had disrupted household work and water supply. “There is no electricity, and there is no water in our homes. How are we supposed to run the water motor without power?” said Rupa, a resident. Residents in Faridabad's New Industrial Township-2 area also took to the streets demanding restoration of power. Police intervened after receiving information about a road blockade and dispersed the protesters after pacifying them. In Nuh, the disruption affected several areas, including Punhana, Nagina and Firozpur Jhirka. Nearly 1,800 manufacturing units hit; industrialists fear losses worth crores The power crisis extended beyond homes, threatening production schedules and deliveries across Gurgaon's industrial belt. Nearly 1,800 manufacturing units in the Sector 37 and Kadipur industrial areas faced disruption after power cuts began around 10pm on Wednesday. Industrial units in Basai were also affected, with manufacturers reporting that machinery had stopped and production lines had come to a halt. The affected businesses include textile units, export houses, auto component manufacturers and suppliers of food to corporate and commercial establishments. Industrialists warned that a prolonged disruption could lead to losses running into crores of rupees, while delays in production could affect the availability of finished goods and timely delivery of supplies. Deepak Maini, chairman of the Progressive Federation of Trade and Industry (PFTI), said there had been no power supply in Sector 37 since 10pm on Wednesday. “Power cuts at industrial units have brought machinery and production to a halt, impacting business operations. With operations suspended across hundreds of units, the risk of losses has increased,” Maini said. Manufacturers attempted to switch to diesel generator sets, but said these could not sustain continuous industrial operations. Generators need cooling breaks after running for several hours, interrupting production and making them unsuitable as a long-term replacement for grid electricity. “A generator is meant for backup, not regular power supply. After running for several hours, it heats up and needs to be switched off to cool down,” industrialist Vikrant Gupta said. The situation was further complicated by the enforcement of GRAP from Wednesday. With restrictions on generator sets intended to control air pollution in the National Capital Region, industrialists said they faced a difficult choice between keeping operations running and complying with pollution-control requirements. Non-compliant generator sets could face action under the applicable norms. “How are we supposed to run our operations amid so many disruptions? Power is basic to running an industry,” another industrialist said. Manufacturers said the crisis had also exposed the difficulties in getting faults repaired when the regular electricity workforce was unavailable. Maini said DHBVN officials had expressed their inability to resolve the problems, while private vendors could not be engaged to work on high-tension lines and feeders. He argued that the immediate priority should be uninterrupted electricity, regardless of the provider. “If DHBVN is unable to provide the service, there is nothing wrong with allowing private players. We want an uninterrupted power supply, whoever provides it — the govt or a private player,” Maini said. He added that frequent outages had already become a persistent problem for manufacturers, requiring repeated maintenance interventions and disrupting production schedules. Industrialist PK Gupta said the responsibility for ensuring electricity supply rested with the government. “It is the govt’s responsibility to ensure power supply. We pay taxes to the govt,” he said. Industrialists urged the state government to consider invoking the Essential Services Maintenance Act (ESMA), if legally warranted, and make alternative arrangements to restore electricity. Their concerns highlighted the immediate economic cost of the strike even as the broader dispute centred on whether a private company should be allowed to distribute electricity alongside the state-owned discom. Old Gurgaon worst hit as feeders remain out of service The disruption was more widespread in DHBVN's Circle 1, which covers Old Gurgaon, sectors 9 and 10, and Kadipur, than in Circle 2, which includes parts of South City, Sohna and sectors along Golf Course Road. In Circle 1, 12 of the 530 11kV feeders were out of service on Thursday. In Circle 2, 14 of the 750 feeders were shut down. In industrial areas, manufacturers turned to diesel generator sets, but these offered only temporary relief, with prolonged use restricted by overheating, cooling requirements and air pollution control norms. The scale of the disruption was reflected in the complaints received by Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam (DHBVN). An official said the department received more than 3,000 complaints within the first 12 hours of the strike, while DHBVN's helplines received around 5,000 outage complaints on Thursday. Gurgaon, which has around 8.5 lakh electricity consumers, saw widespread disruption, particularly in Old Gurgaon. Residents said more than 50,000 households in the area were affected on Thursday, with several localities continuing to face outages even after hours of waiting. The agitation also affected Faridabad and Nuh, where residential areas and industrial units reported power cuts. Industrialists said repeated calls to DHBVN officials had failed to resolve the disruption, leaving workers and machinery idle No electricity, no water For thousands of families, the immediate concern was no longer just the absence of electricity but the inability to carry out everyday activities, from cooking and studying to securing drinking water. In Sector 9A, around 6,000 families were affected after power supply snapped around 3.30am on Thursday. The outage also affected the boosting station supplying the area, leaving households without water. More than 16 hours later, supply had still not been restored, according to Suraj Bhola, general secretary of the Sector 9A residents' welfare association (RWA). “I have called the officials nearly 50 times, but nobody is responding. There is no electricity at our homes. Inverters have run out, and now there is no water either because the boosting station is affected. How are people supposed to manage their daily needs?” Bhola said. - General picture of Industrial workers.______________Picture by TOI He alleged that the junior engineer was not answering calls, while the sub-divisional officer had cited the strike. The helpline number provided by the district administration had also failed to secure relief, he said. With no clarity on when electricity would return, residents were unable to plan their day or arrange alternative water supplies. Tankers, he added, were also difficult to find. In Hari Nagar, more than 7,000 families were affected after power supply went off around 10pm on Wednesday and remained disrupted for more than 16 hours, residents said. The accompanying water shortage left families struggling to meet basic needs. “People are suffering in their homes, children are struggling to study, and nobody is listening to us. Junior engineer (JE) and SDO are not answering calls. The office has been locked, and there is nobody available to address the complaints,” said Sumit Gujjar, Hari Nagar RWA president. While acknowledging employees' right to protest, Gujjar questioned the impact of the agitation on ordinary residents. “If employees have an issue with the govt, they should take it up with the govt instead of leaving residents without electricity and water,” he said. At Zara Aavaas, an affordable housing society, residents said power had been unavailable since 5.30am. The backup system covered essential services such as lifts but did not provide electricity to individual flats. Many residents have to work from home, but how are they supposed to work without electricity for so many hours? It is even more difficult for people with medical conditions who may depend on electrical equipment or need a comfortable indoor environment,” he said. Residents of Lotus Homz also struggled as the outage continued through the day. “There has been no power supply since 5am. It has become difficult to manage even basic household chores. The Australian green tree frog ( Pelodryas caerulea ), also known as simply green tree frog in Australia, White's tree frog , or dumpy tree frog , is a species of tree frog native to Australia and New Guinea , with introduced populations in the United States and New Zealand, though the latter is believed to have died out. It is morphologically similar to some other members of its family, particularly the magnificent tree frog ( P. splendida ) and the white-lipped tree frog ( Sandyrana infrafrenata ).

Larger than most Australian frogs , the Australian green tree frog reaches 10 cm (4 in) or more in length. Its average lifespan in captivity, about 16 years, is long compared with most frogs. Docile and well suited to living near human dwellings, Australian green tree frogs are often found on window sills or inside houses, eating insects drawn by the light. The green tree frog screams when it is in danger to scare off its foe, and squeaks when it is touched.

Due to its appearance and behavioural traits, the green tree frog is a popular exotic pet throughout the world. The skin secretions of the frog have antibacterial and antiviral properties that may prove useful in pharmaceutical preparations and which have rendered it relatively immune to the population declines being experienced by many species of amphibian . It is a common species and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has assessed its conservation status as being " least concern ".

The Australian green tree frog is a member of the family Pelodryadidae , which is endemic to Australia and New Guinea. [ 2 ] The common name of the species, "White's tree frog", is in honour of John White 's first description in 1790. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] The green tree frog was the first Australian frog to be scientifically described ; the original specimen found its way into the collection of Sir Joseph Banks , but was destroyed when the Hunterian Museum in London was bombed in World War II. [ 5 ]

The species was originally called the "blue frog" ( Rana caerulea ) despite its green colour. The specimens White sent to England were damaged by the preservative and appeared blue. [ 3 ] The colour of the frog is caused by blue and green pigments covered in a yellow layer; the preservative destroyed the yellow layer and left the frog with a blue appearance. The specific epithet, caerulea , which is Latin for blue, has remained. [ 6 ] This frog is often referred to as Litoria caerulea in the scientific literature. [ 6 ] In Australia, the frog is also known more simply as the "green tree frog", but that name is often given to the most common green arboreal species in a region, such as the American green tree frog ( Hyla cinerea ).

A 2020 study showed that Pelodryas caerulea is actually a species complex that includes recently identified species such as Pelodryas mira , which is endemic to New Guinea . [ 7 ]

The green tree frog is a plump, rather large tree frog, and can grow up to 11.5 cm (4.5 in) in length, with fully grown females being slightly larger than males. A distinctive fatty ridge is seen over the eye, and the parotoid gland is moderately large. The iris is golden and has a horizontally slit pupil, and the tympanum (a skin membrane similar to an eardrum ) is visible just behind the eye. Selective breeding has also resulted in blue irises. The forelimbs are short and robust while the hind limbs extend to be very long, and large, circular adhesive discs at the end of each digit provide grip while climbing. The fingers are about one-third webbed, and the toes nearly three-quarters webbed. The dorsal colour depends on the temperature and nature of the environment, ranging from brown, brownish- or greyish-green, to bright emerald green. Selective breeding in captivity has also resulted in "honey"-toned individuals whose colors vary from mauve to pale yellow. The frog occasionally has small, irregularly shaped white spots on its back. Selective breeding in captivity has resulted in individuals with a greater number of these white spots. Males have a wrinkled vocal sac under the throat which can vary in color from grey to yellow, while the throat of females is white and the skin is more taut. The ventral surface in both sexes is creamy-white and rough in texture. [ 3 ] [ 8 ]

This frog is similar in appearance to the magnificent tree frog ( R. splendida ), which inhabits only north-western Australia. Older members of that species have very large parotoid glands, which cover the entire top of their heads and droop over their tympana. The parotoid gland of the green tree frog is much smaller, and it also lacks the yellow speckling on the back and the yellow markings on the hand, groin, and thigh. [ 9 ] It can be distinguished from the white-lipped tree frog (giant tree frog N. infrafrenatus ) by the distinct white stripe that species has along the edge of the lower jaw and extending to the shoulder, which is not present in the green tree frog. [ 10 ]

Some arboreal hylid frogs benefit from two hygroscopically-enabled hydration processes : transcutaneous uptake of condensation on their skin and reduced evaporative water loss. Their wiping behaviour spreads hygroscopic secretions from the parotoid gland across their skin, facilitating both methods. [ 11 ] P. caerulea ' s skin structure, the hygroscopic coating, and an advantageous temperature gradient combine to boost condensation and moisture uptake.

The tadpoles' appearance changes throughout their development. When newly hatched, they are 8 mm (0.3 in) long and when fully developed, 44 mm (1.7 in) . They are initially mottled with brown, and increase in pigmentation (to either green or brown) during development. Their undersides are initially dark, but later become lighter in hue. The eggs are brown and are wrapped in a clear jelly; they are 1.1 to 1.4 mm (0.043 to 0.055 in) in diameter. [ 6 ]

The call is a low, slow brawk-brawk-brawk , repeated many times. For most of the year, the frogs call from high positions, such as trees and gutters, but during the breeding season, they descend to near the ponds and pools, where they breed. Like many frogs, green tree frogs call not only to attract a mate, but also to advertise their location outside the mating season. They are particularly vocal after rain, but the reasons for this are unclear. They emit a stress call when they are in danger, such as when being attacked by a predator or when a person steps on the log in which one is concealed. [ 8 ]

The green tree frog is native to northern and eastern regions of Australia and to the lowlands of New Guinea. Distribution is limited mostly to areas with warm, wet tropical climates. Its range spans from Irian Jaya to Port Moresby , and is most abundant on Daru Island . The IUCN suggests "scattered locations" in both New Guinea and Indonesia. [ 1 ] In Australia, its range extends from the Kimberley region of Western Australia through the Northern Territory and Queensland to north and central New South Wales and the extreme northeasterly part of South Australia . Its total extent of land occupancy is around 4,078,600 square kilometres (1,574,800 sq mi) . [ 12 ]

The species has been introduced to both the United States and New Zealand. In the United States, it is restricted to two regions within Florida , where it was possibly introduced through the pet trade . Only small populations have been found there, and whether they have caused any ecological damage as an invasive species is unknown. [ 13 ] In New Zealand, several individuals were liberated in various locations in 1897 and 1899, and a further accidental introduction was made in the 1940s. No sightings have been reported of this species since the 1950s. [ 14 ]

Depending on their location, green tree frogs occupy various habitats. They prefer moist forests but are not strictly limited to tropical rainforests. [ 8 ] They are often found in the canopy of trees near water bodies, but also occupy terrestrial habitats well away from water. They favour old stands of Eucalyptus , where the trees have hollows in which water collects. They are common along inland waterways and can survive in swamps (among the reeds ) or in grasslands in cooler climates. [ 15 ]

Green tree frogs are little troubled by the presence of humans and often live in close association with them. They sometimes stray inside houses and are found in such places as sinks and toilets. They can also be found on outside windowsills at night, eating insects attracted to the light, and they may gather under outdoor lighting for the same reason. [ 3 ] [ 15 ] They sometimes occupy tanks ( cisterns ), downpipes (downspouts), and gutters, as these have high humidity and are usually cooler than the external environment. They may be drawn to the downpipes and tanks during the mating season because the fixtures amplify their calls. [ 8 ] Green tree frogs seem to have homing abilities, being able to return to locations from which they were caught from a considerable distance after being displaced. [ 5 ]

Australian green tree frogs are very docile and unafraid of humans. [ 8 ] They are nocturnal [ 3 ] and come out in early evenings to call (in spring and summer) and hunt for food. During the day, they find cool, dark, and moist areas, such as tree holes or rock crevices, in which to sleep. They are not a rainforest species, but make use of the rain that falls almost daily and collects on leaves and in crevices, to keep themselves moist. Their skin exudes a waxy coating that helps prevent evaporation. In dry periods, they avoid desiccation by concealing themselves in a cool spot, perhaps by burrowing, and enveloping themselves in a cocoon made of shed skin and mucus . [ 8 ] While there is insufficient evidence proving that they are a social species, they have also been shown to gather together in "clumps" while sleeping, possibly to conserve moisture through skin-to-skin contact.

The diet of the green tree frog consists mainly of insects such as moths , cockroaches , and locusts . They also eat spiders and can include smaller frogs and even small mammals (including bats, such as little bent-wing bats , microbats and other unidentified bats [ 16 ] ) among their prey. [ 6 ] [ 8 ] Frog teeth are not suited to cutting up prey, so the food item must be small enough to fit inside its mouth.

Many frogs flick out their sticky tongues at prey and the victim sticks to the tip and is drawn back into the mouth and consumed. A green tree frog uses this technique for smaller prey; for larger items, however, it pounces, then pushes the prey into its mouth with its hands. [ 5 ]

The frog has a few native predators, among them snakes and birds . Since the European settlement of Australia , non-native predators have been introduced, primarily dogs and cats. [ 17 ] The species has an average life expectancy in captivity of 16 years, but some have been known to live over 20 years. [ 8 ]

Breeding occurs between November and February. [ 12 ] During the mating season, the males call from slightly elevated positions close to the still-water sources in which they choose to breed. [ 8 ] Clumps of between 200 and 2000 eggs are laid which initially float, but sink within 24 hours. The development of the tadpoles takes about six weeks, after which they undergo metamorphosis and leave the water as juvenile frogs.

The green tree frog is one of the most popular pet frogs throughout the world. Its docile nature and long life expectancy make it an attractive choice for exotic pet owners. It is also one of the easier frogs to maintain; its diet is broad and it has a strong resistance to disease. One problem commonly associated with keeping this species as a pet is overfeeding; green tree frogs tend to become obese if overfed. In the wild, exertion of energy is required for a frog to capture its prey. However, in captivity, they are usually given live feed in a confined space. This lessens the activity needed for feeding, resulting in weight gain. An overweight member of the species deposits fat layers over the top of the head and body, giving it a "dumpy" appearance, thus the name "dumpy tree frog". [ 8 ] [ 18 ]

The rover fireflies of the genus Photinus (including the common eastern firefly of North America ) are poisonous to these frogs, and an incident has been reported in which a firefly was fed to a green tree frog, which subsequently died. [ 19 ]

Australian law gives protected status to the green tree frog—along with all Australian fauna —under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 . [ 20 ] The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the green tree frog's conservation status as being of " least concern ", given its broad range, its large total population, and its tolerance of a variety of habitat types. The population trend seems to be stable, and any decline in numbers is not likely to be at a fast enough rate to justify listing it in a more threatened category. [ 1 ]

In suburban areas, this frog is threatened by pollution and by predation by domestic animals. Also, some of the frogs have been found to be infected with the chytrid fungus which causes the fatal amphibian disease chytridiomycosis . The frog's status in New Guinea is poorly studied, but in 2002, some 75,000 individuals were exported from Indonesia as part of the pet trade, and this may impact populations in some locations. The frog is present in a number of protected areas in New Guinea, and it has been successfully bred in some Australian zoos. Overall, the main threat to this species is the potential for a widespread disease epidemic. [ 1 ]

Although frogs have lungs, they absorb oxygen through their skin; for this to occur efficiently, the skin must be moist. A disadvantage of moist skin is that pathogens such as molds and bacteria can thrive on it, increasing the chance of infection. To counteract this, frogs secrete peptides that destroy these pathogens. The secretion from the paratoid gland of the green tree frog contains 25 caerins, a group of peptides with antibacterial and antiviral properties. The caerins produced by frogs of this species from different geographical localities have subtle but reproducible differences. [ 21 ] The secretions also contain caeruleins , which have the same physiological effects as CCK-8 , a digestive hormone and hunger suppressant. [ 22 ] These caeruleins now have a number of clinical applications. [ 5 ] Several peptides from the skin secretions of the green tree frog have been found to destroy HIV without harming healthy T cells . [ 23 ] [ 24 ] [ 25 ]

The fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis , the causal agent of chytridiomycosis, is causing declines in many species of amphibians, but the secretions produced by the green tree frog and certain other Australian species of frog ( Chlorohyla chloris and Spicicalyx serrata ) are protective against this fungus. The peptides inhibit the growth of the fungus in vitro and these frog species are believed not to be in decline. [ 26 ]

Green tree frogs are sometimes used as model animals in research. [ 27 ] The structure of their toe pads was used to investigate the microstructure and properties of the epithelium that allows the animals to adhere to wet surfaces. [ 28 ]
